sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot xv (printed pp. 261–263)
rows: [p. 261] Ereu. Nolite me in novam vocare operam. [Margin: Nodus XV. Caeterorum planetarum rationes ex dictis aestimari posse.] Haec enim iam expedita est. Expressimus enim in his quomodo mediante sole, tres motus fiant, in longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem, secundum tres perpendiculares quibus quanti species crescunt. Satis itaque constabit vobis alios motus nullos esse posse, a centro in circumferentiam (quales sunt qui a sole in Planetas proficiscantur) pos-[p. 262]sunt itaque motuum alii numeri in aliis Planetis reperiri: sed qui a causis aliis, id est, saltem non Analogis proficiscantur, difficile persuadeat.

[p. 261] Ereu. Do not [Nolite] call me into a new labour [operam]. [Margin: Knot XV. That the accounts [rationes] of the other planets can be estimated [aestimari] from the things said.] For this [Haec] is already dispatched [expedita]. For we have expressed in these [things] how, the sun mediating [mediante sole], three motions come about [fiant], into length [longitudinem], breadth [latitudinem], and depth [profunditatem], according to the three perpendiculars by which the species of quantity [quanti species] grow. It will therefore be sufficiently evident [constabit] to you that no other motions can be, from the centre into the circumference (such as are [those] which proceed from the sun into the Planets); there [p. 262] can therefore be found other numbers of motions in other Planets: but [that there are any] which proceed from other causes, that is, at least not from Analogous [Analogis] [ones], [one] would with difficulty persuade [difficile persuadeat].

Frustra itaque me eorum motibus immittam, in quibus nihil particularis quod constet, adhuc repererunt Astronomi, neque cum repererint facile de iis iudicare, nisi ex proportione ad haec licebit. Quod enim a sole sint illarum motus vix potest dubitari. Cum lumen & calorem id est vitam ab eo recipiant. Est itaque motus eorum conversio ad ipsum. Si autem ab ipso, cum notum sit actionem ignis esse separationem humidi a sicco, constabit ex aliqua vaporum elevatione futurum. Caetera ex particularibus circumstantiis globorum dependent. Ego vero rem satis me dignam exegisse opinor, si admirationem qua hos motus quasi ex machina factos suspiciunt, paululum minuerim, tractabilesque etiam eorum esse causas quasi digito monstraverim.

In vain therefore shall I send myself into [immittam] their motions, in which the Astronomers have as yet found nothing particular which may be established [quod constet], nor, when they shall have found [it], will it be permitted [licebit] to judge easily of them, unless out of proportion to these [things]. For that the motions of those [illarum] are from the sun can scarcely be doubted. Since they receive light and heat, that is, life, from it. The motion of them therefore is a turning [conversio] towards it. But if [it is] from it, since it is known that the action of fire is the separation of the moist [humidi] from the dry [sicco], it will be evident [constabit] [that it] will come about [futurum] out of some elevation of vapours. The rest [Caetera] depend on the particular circumstances of the globes. But I think I have accomplished [exegisse] a thing sufficiently worthy of me, if I shall have diminished a little the wonder [admirationem] with which they look up at [suspiciunt] these motions as though made out of a machine [quasi ex machina], and shall have shown as it were with a finger that their causes also are tractable [tractabiles].

[Margin, beside the preceding lines: Solem circa suum centrum moveri.] Non superest modo nisi reliquorum Architectus sol, quem motu circulari citra centrum versari, nullo autem alio moderni Astronomi contendunt. Nec immerito: cum enim natura ipsius ignea sit & ebulliens: si non in circulum versaretur, flammis {?emicantibus} variegatae cuiusdam figurae appareret, quae nunc motu circulari retro latae corpus allambunt, & sphaericam lucis nobis [p. 263] speciem exhibent. Si autem super alio centro veheretur, comarum longum Syrma traheret.

[Margin, beside the preceding lines: That the Sun is moved about its own centre.] There does not remain now [anything] except the Architect [Architectus] of the rest, the sun, which the modern Astronomers contend is turned [versari] with circular motion about [citra, printed; read circa] the centre, but with no other. Nor undeservedly: for since its nature is fiery and boiling-up [ebulliens]: if it were not turned into a circle, it would appear [as being] of a certain figure variegated [variegatae] with {?darting} [emicantibus] flames, which now, carried back [retro latae] by the circular motion, lick around [allambunt] the body, and exhibit to us a spherical [p. 263] appearance [speciem] of light. But if it were carried upon another centre, it would draw a long Train [Syrma] of hairs [comarum].

Argumenta Astronomica ex Galilaeo & aliis qui de systemate coeli scripserunt, petenda relinquo. Unum hoc si tibi, Andabata suggessero. Si habes amicum aliquem Astronomiae studiosum, age cum ipso, ut sicut in chartis orbis terrarum navigationem alicuius aliquando pictores punctis ordine sitis deducunt: sic Planetarum tibi in papyro cursus, ipsorum inquam discorum non orbium cum suis proportionibus ex Ptolemaico & Copernicano systemate depingat, & utrumque cum consideraveris, nisi sapientem illum Hispanum (quem solent impietatis insimulare quod dixerit si potestatem parem scientiae possideret, se mundo ordinem eo quem tunc pro rato habebant, potiorem tributurum) ipse tu piissimum dicas, eosque contra impios qui sapientissimo Deo tam deforme & perturbatum organum tribuunt, me pro insipido & harum rerum ignaro arbitro habeto. [Margin: Ex solo visu motuum Copernici & Ptolomei in sphaera materiali iudicium ferri posse de quaestione.]

The Astronomical arguments I leave to be sought from Galilaeus and others who have written on the system of the heaven. This one [thing] if I shall have suggested to you, Andabata [— it will suffice]. If you have some friend studious of Astronomy, deal [age] with him, that, just as on charts [chartis] of the circle of lands [orbis terrarum] painters sometimes trace out [deducunt] the navigation of someone by points set in order: so he may depict for you on paper the courses of the Planets, of the discs [discorum] themselves, I say, not of the orbs [orbium], with their proportions, out of the Ptolemaic and Copernican system; and when you shall have considered both, unless you yourself call that wise Spaniard (whom they are wont to accuse [insimulare] of impiety, because he said [that], if he possessed power equal to [his] knowledge, he would assign [tributurum] to the world an order preferable [potiorem] to that which they then held as ratified [pro rato]) most pious, and those, on the contrary [contra], impious, who attribute to the most wise God so misshapen [deforme] and disturbed an instrument [organum], hold me for an insipid [insipido] judge [arbitro] and ignorant of these things. [Margin: That from the sight alone of the motions of Copernicus and Ptolemy in a material sphere [in sphaera materiali] a judgement can be brought [ferri] on the question.]
[p. 264 blank. Dialogue III, ‘De duratione & gubernatione Mundi’, begins on p. 265.]

terms: ‘quanti’ could be misread as ‘how great’ (quanti species crescunt ‘how great the species grow’); here genitive of quantum, ‘the quantum, quantity’.

Aristotelian/scholastic: length, breadth and depth are the three dimensions of continuous quantity (Categories 6; Physics IV); White grounds the three planetary motions (longitude, latitude, distance) in the three dimensions.
The pun is deliberate: geometrical dimensions = the planetary coordinates.
‘by means of the sun’, ‘through the sun’s agency’
Scholastic ‘medium’ of causation; the sun is the instrumental cause of planetary motion in White’s (Digbean) mechanics.
Mathematical/analogical sense: other planets’ motions are explained by causes proportional to those of the Earth and Moon.
Also echoes Neoplatonic/scholastic ‘conversio’ of an effect to its source; physically = circling the sun.
the separation of the moist from the dry
Peripatetic/Digbean definition of the action of fire (heat rarefies and draws off moisture as vapour).
as though made out of a machine
‘as if by a stage-machine’ (deus ex machina), i.e. miraculously; or ‘by clockwork’
White wants to reduce wonder at the motions as if they were contrived; may glance at the theatrical machine.
Both literal (gazing at the sky) and figurative senses fit.
The sun as the organising cause of the other motions.
Probably a misprint: the margin has ‘circa suum centrum’. Sun’s axial rotation known from Galileo’s and Scheiner’s sunspot observations (1612–30).
Rare compound (ad + lambo); flames licking the body of the sun.
As in earlier units (comet terms): a sun moved off-centre would trail like a comet.
Classical idiom; ‘charts of the world’ = maps on which a voyage is traced.
of the discs, not of the orbs
visible bodies vs. supposed solid spheres
White insists on drawing the real paths of planetary bodies, not the fictitious solid orbs (cf. D2-N14).
Margin speaks of a model; the text of drawing on paper.

Alfonso X ‘el Sabio’ of Castile (1221–84), patron of the Alfonsine Tables, to whom was attributed the saying that had he been present at the Creation he would have advised a simpler order; often cited as impious. White turns it into piety against the complexity of Ptolemaic astronomy.
The cosmos as God’s instrument; a ‘deformed and disturbed’ machine is unworthy of a wise God.
Wordplay with sapiens/sapientissimo (sapere ‘to taste, be wise’).
notes: Unit: Dialogue II, Knot xv (complete in one part; the last knot of Dialogue II). PDF pp. 272–274 = printed pp. 261–263; p. 264 (PDF 275) is blank. Offset +11 holds (running heads 261, 262, 263; 265 on PDF 276). Knot xv begins with ‘Ereu. Nolite me in novam vocare operam’ (margin ‘Nodus XV.’, p. 261) and ends with Dialogue II on p. 263. The margin title (‘Caeterorum planetarum rationes ex dictis aestimari posse’) differs from the FM2 table (‘Caeterorum Planetarum motus ex declaratis posse aestimari’).
Dialogue III’s heading on p. 265 reads ‘De duratione & gubernatione Mundi’, not ‘de causis Mundi’ as in the FM2 table; to be noted in D3-N01.

Uncertain readings: (1) ‘emic[ant]ibus’ — a blot covers two letters on p. 262; read {?emicantibus}. (2) ‘citra centrum’ is clearly printed, but ‘circa’ (as in the margin) is required by sense; translated as circa with the printed word bracketed. (3) The sentence ‘Satis itaque constabit … possunt itaque motuum alii numeri … difficile persuadeat’ is syntactically loose (two ‘itaque’, no conjunction before ‘possunt’); kept as printed and rendered clause by clause. (4) ‘illarum motus’ — feminine, perhaps referring to stellae understood; rendered ‘of those [illarum]’. (5) ‘Unum hoc si tibi … suggessero’ is elliptical; ‘[— it will suffice]’ supplied.

Verification pass: 3 corrections after the sentence-by-sentence check — (1) ‘eosque contra impios’ re-read with ‘contra’ as adverb (‘and those, on the contrary, impious, who attribute…’) rather than the preposition ‘against the impious’; (2) ‘quanti species’ rendered ‘the species of quantity’ (genitive of quantum), not ‘how great the species’; (3) ‘flammis … variegatae’ construed together (‘variegated with flames’), not ‘flames’ as a separate ablative of means for ‘appareret’. Transcription re-checked against 300-dpi crops of pp. 261–263 (quanti, citra, margins of pp. 262–263).

Conventions: as in earlier units — long s normalised, æ/œ/ę → ae/oe (Hęc → Haec, Cętera → Caetera), accents dropped, u/v normalised to v, macrons expanded (cētrum → centrum, motuū → motuum); Ptolomei (margin) and Galilaeo kept as printed; supplied words in [square brackets]; Latin of technical or ambiguous words in [brackets].
